section.title: The Burnt Offering
section.sectionRationale: Leviticus opens the first great collection of sacrificial law, the instructions for the burnt offering, which the LORD speaks to Moses from the newly erected Tent of Meeting at the end of Exodus. This is the offering wholly given to God, and it sets the pattern followed by the offerings that come after it.
section.thesis: The burnt offering teaches Israel that approach to a holy God requires an unblemished substitute, the laying on of hands, the shedding of blood, and a total surrender of the whole animal to God, whether the worshiper brings a costly bull or the humble bird of the poor.
section.frameNote: Three movements, one for each kind of offering: the burnt offering from the herd, from the flock, and from the birds, each ending in the same phrase, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

units.label: The offering from the herd
units.note: an unblemished male, hands laid on its head

verses.text: Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying,
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When any of you brings an {{korban|offering}} to the LORD, you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock.
If one's offering is a {{olah|burnt offering}} from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male. He must bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD.
He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, so it can be accepted on his behalf to {{kipper|make atonement}} for him.
And he shall slaughter the young bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests are to present the blood and sprinkle it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Next, he is to skin the burnt offering and cut it into pieces.
The sons of Aaron the priest shall put a fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire.
Then Aaron's sons the priests are to arrange the pieces, including the head and the fat, atop the burning wood on the altar.
The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a {{nichoach|pleasing aroma}} to the LORD.

units.label: The offering from the flock
units.note: sheep or goats, the same pattern

verses.text: If, however, one's offering is a burnt offering from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he is to present an unblemished male.
He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests are to sprinkle its blood against the altar on all sides.
He is to cut the animal into pieces, and the priest shall arrange them, including the head and fat, atop the burning wood that is on the altar.
The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall bring all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
If, instead, one's offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.
Then the priest shall bring it to the altar, twist off its head, and burn it on the altar; its blood should be drained out on the side of the altar.
And he is to remove the crop with its contents and throw it to the east side of the altar, in the place for ashes.

He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely. And the priest is to burn it on the altar atop the burning wood. It is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

korban.gloss: An offering, from a root meaning to draw near. The word itself teaches that sacrifice exists to bring the worshiper near to God, not merely to dispose of an animal. Every offering in Leviticus is a qorban, a means of approach to the LORD.

olah.gloss: The burnt offering, from a root meaning to go up. The whole animal, except the hide, ascends to God in smoke, so nothing is retained for the worshiper. It pictures total, unreserved consecration offered to the LORD.

kipper.gloss: To atone, to cover or make amends. The laying on of hands identifies the worshiper with the animal, so that its death is accepted in his place, covering the offense that separated him from God.

nichoach.gloss: A pleasing or soothing aroma. The phrase describes God's acceptance of the offering, not that He needs food, but that the sacrifice, rightly offered, is received with favor rather than turned away in judgment.

basic.context: Leviticus opens with God speaking to Moses from the newly built Tent of Meeting, right where Exodus left off. The first instructions concern the burnt offering, the sacrifice that is burned up entirely as a gift to God. Whether an Israelite brought a costly bull or, if poor, only a bird, the pattern was the same: an unblemished animal, hands laid on its head, blood shed, and the whole thing given over to God.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes the actual sacrificial system God gave Israel under the old covenant; it does not prescribe animal sacrifice for believers today. Its abiding truth is that sinful people cannot approach a holy God empty handed, and that atonement requires a substitute who dies in the worshiper's place.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for offering, qorban, comes from a root meaning to draw near, showing that sacrifice exists to bring people to God. The olah, burnt offering, goes up entirely in smoke, holding nothing back. And kaphar, to atone, describes the laying on of hands that transfers the worshiper's standing onto the animal that dies for him.
basic.typology: The unblemished animal, wholly consumed, foreshadows Christ, who offered Himself without spot to God and held nothing of Himself back. The provision of a lesser offering for the poor, turtledoves or pigeons, foreshadows a gospel that excludes no one for lack of means; the same atonement is available to rich and poor alike.
basic.christ: Hebrews calls Christ's sacrifice better than the blood of bulls and goats, since His offering actually takes away sin rather than merely covering it until the next year. Where the burnt offering had to be repeated, Jesus offered Himself once for all, and gave Himself wholly, holding nothing back, exactly as the burnt offering pictured.
basic.god: God is holy, so approach to Him is never casual; a substitute must die. Yet He is also gracious, providing a way in even for the poor, since the required offering scales down to a pair of birds for anyone who cannot afford a bull or lamb. His holiness never becomes an excuse to exclude the poor from His presence.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 10:1-10 says these sacrifices could never take away sins, and that Christ came to do God's will once for all. Romans 12:1 calls believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, echoing the total surrender of the burnt offering. John 1:29 calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
basic.oneStory: The burnt offering teaches, at the very start of Leviticus, that a holy God can only be approached through a substitute who dies in the worshiper's place and is wholly given over to Him. That pattern of atoning substitution and total consecration reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the once for all sacrifice who opens the way to God for everyone, however little they bring.

context.literary:
Leviticus begins with a conjunction, 'Then the LORD called to Moses,' and its Hebrew title, Vayyiqra, is simply that first word, 'and He called.' The book is a continuation, not a fresh start. Exodus 40:35 left Moses outside a tent he could not enter; Leviticus 1:1 has the LORD summon him and speak from inside it. What follows in chapters 1 to 7 is God's own answer to the question the end of Exodus raises: how can a people live near a glory like that?

Chapter 1 is a single speech with a short introduction, verse 2, and three cases, each introduced by 'if': from the herd, verses 3 to 9, from the flock, verses 10 to 13, and of birds, verses 14 to 17. Each case closes with the same formula, 'a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD,' verses 9, 13 and 17. The repetition works like a refrain, and it tells the reader that the three offerings, unequal in cost, are equal in result.

The cases shrink as they go. The herd offering is described in full, step by step. The flock offering assumes much of that procedure and adds only what differs, such as the north side of the altar, verse 11. The bird offering needs a different procedure altogether because a bird is too small to be laid on, skinned or cut in pieces, so the priest does nearly everything, verses 15 to 17. The text is written as case law, as practical as a manual, yet the refrain lifts each case to the same height.

There is also a rhythm of shared work. The worshiper presents, lays his hand, slaughters, skins, cuts and washes. The priests handle the blood, the fire, the wood and the altar. Every step is 'before the LORD,' verses 3, 5 and 11. The burnt offering comes first among the offerings of chapters 1 to 7, likely because it was the regular offering of the altar, made every morning and evening, Exodus 29:38-42, and because the others are burned 'atop the burnt offering,' Leviticus 3:5.
context.historical:
These words were given at Sinai within weeks of the tabernacle's dedication, between the first day of the first month, Exodus 40:17, and the first day of the second month, Numbers 1:1. The priests are already called 'Aaron's sons,' though their ordination is not recorded until Leviticus 8, so the law anticipates the service it will govern.

Burnt offerings were far older than Sinai. Noah offered them after the flood, Genesis 8:20, and Job offered them for his children, Job 1:5. Abraham was told to offer Isaac 'as a burnt offering,' Genesis 22:2, and offered a ram 'in place of his son,' Genesis 22:13. Israel's neighbours offered them too. Balaam stood Balak 'by your burnt offering,' Numbers 23:3, and the king of Moab once 'offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall,' 2 Kings 3:27. Against that background Leviticus 1 is as notable for what it excludes as for what it commands. Only clean domestic animals and birds are named, and the whole world of human sacrifice is shut out, as Deuteronomy 12:31 says plainly.

The three options map onto an agricultural economy. A bull from the herd was the most valuable animal a farmer owned, the source of ploughing and of calves. Sheep and goats were the common wealth of a household. Turtledoves and young pigeons were within reach of almost anyone. Elsewhere the law makes the concession explicit for those who 'cannot afford a lamb,' Leviticus 5:7 and 12:8, and Mary and Joseph brought exactly that offering when Jesus was presented at the temple, Luke 2:24.

The setting is the courtyard. The worshiper came to 'the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' verse 3, the space between the gate and the altar. The tabernacle faced east, Exodus 27:13, so the ash heap 'on the east side of the altar,' verse 16, lay toward the entrance, and later the ashes were carried 'outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place,' Leviticus 6:11. The hide went to the officiating priest, Leviticus 7:8, the only part of the animal not burned.
context.canonical:
The burnt offering runs through the whole Old Testament as the basic act of worship. It was the regular sacrifice of every morning and evening, Exodus 29:38-42 and Numbers 28:3-6, and the fire under it was never to go out, Leviticus 6:12-13. When Aaron offered the first sacrifices, fire came from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering, Leviticus 9:24, as it did again on Carmel, 1 Kings 18:38. David refused to offer 'burnt offerings that cost me nothing,' 2 Samuel 24:24.

The prophets and psalmists then guard the offering from misuse. 'Obedience is better than sacrifice,' Samuel tells Saul, 1 Samuel 15:22. God says through Hosea, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings,' Hosea 6:6. Psalm 51 holds both sides: 'You take no pleasure in burnt offerings,' yet when the heart is broken and contrite, 'Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings,' Psalm 51:16-19. Psalm 50 denies that God needs food at all, 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you,' Psalm 50:12. The critique is not of the burnt offering as God gave it, but of offerings cut loose from faith and obedience.

The New Testament takes up the offering in three ways. A scribe agrees with Jesus that loving God and neighbour 'is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices,' Mark 12:33. Hebrews reads Psalm 40:6-8 as the words of Christ: 'In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. Then I said, Here I am... I have come to do Your will,' Hebrews 10:5-10. The obedient life and death of the Son is the offering the animals pointed to. And the language of the burnt offering is applied to Christian life: Christ gave Himself 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2, believers offer their bodies 'as living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1, and a church's gift to a missionary is 'a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice,' Philippians 4:18.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that the God who had just filled the tabernacle could be approached, and how. The opening case law assumes the initiative lies with the worshiper, 'When any of you brings an offering,' verse 2, yet every detail of how it is done lies with God. Nothing is left to invention.

He meant them to feel the seriousness of approach. The worshiper does the killing himself, 'he shall slaughter the young bull before the LORD,' verse 5. He watches the blood splashed on the altar and the animal burned entire. No one could offer a burnt offering and think that coming to God was a light matter. Sin and death were not abstractions at this altar.

He also meant them to see the goal: acceptance. The word appears at the start, 'for its acceptance before the LORD,' verse 3, and 'so it can be accepted on his behalf,' verse 4, and the refrain at the end says the same thing another way, 'a pleasing aroma.' The worshiper did not come to placate an angry deity with a meal but to be received by a holy God on the ground He provided.

And he meant every Israelite to know that access did not depend on wealth. The three cases make the poorest man's single dove as fully a burnt offering as the rich man's bull.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Leviticus 1 is prescriptive law for Israel, but it is law for a sanctuary and priesthood that no longer exist, and the New Testament says why they have ended. Hebrews teaches that these sacrifices, offered 'again and again,' could 'never take away sins,' and that Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and sat down, Hebrews 10:11-12. To bring an animal to an altar now would be to treat His offering as incomplete.

So the chapter's commands do not carry over as practice. What carries over is what the New Testament itself draws out. Christians offer themselves, 'your bodies as living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1. They give in ways that cost them, as David insisted, 2 Samuel 24:24, and they bring God their best rather than the blemished leftovers Malachi condemned, Malachi 1:8. Above all, they approach God only through the offering He has provided and accepted.

The chapter also warns against reading its details for private symbolism. The north side of the altar and the ash heap on the east side were arrangements of the courtyard, and the text gives them no symbolic meaning. Application should follow the lines Scripture draws, not ones we invent.

debates.question: What does the laying on of the hand in verse 4 mean?

views.label: Transfer of sin to the substitute
views.case: The gesture is joined immediately to atonement, 'so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him,' verse 4. On the Day of Atonement Aaron lays both hands on the goat, confesses Israel's sins and puts them 'on the goat's head,' Leviticus 16:21. A long line of interpreters has seen the same movement here: guilt laid on the victim, which then dies in the worshiper's place.

views.label: Identification and ownership
views.case: Others note that verse 4 uses one hand, not the two hands of Leviticus 16:21, and that no confession is mentioned. The gesture then marks the animal as this worshiper's own offering, so that what happens to it counts for him. Laying on of hands elsewhere designates or appoints, as with the Levites, Numbers 8:10.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A third view combines them: the hand says 'this animal stands for me,' and because it stands for the worshiper, its death is accepted as atonement on his behalf. Identification is the means; substitution is the result.

debates.bearing: The text does not describe what the worshiper thought or said, but it ties the hand directly to acceptance and atonement. At the least the animal represents the worshiper before God, and its death is received in his favour, a pattern the New Testament sees fulfilled in the One who 'gave Himself up for me,' Galatians 2:20.

debates.question: If the sin offering deals with specific sins, what does the burnt offering atone for?

views.label: General sinfulness before a holy God
views.case: The burnt offering was offered before any sin offering existed, by Noah and Job, and Job offered it because 'Perhaps my children have sinned,' Job 1:5. On this reading it covers the general condition of a sinful person coming near a holy God, while the sin and guilt offerings of chapters 4 to 6 deal with particular offences.

views.label: Chiefly a gift of devotion, with atonement secondary
views.case: Others stress that the burnt offering is voluntary, 'When any of you brings,' verse 2, and that its refrain is the pleasing aroma. It is mainly an act of worship and self-offering, and the mention of atonement in verse 4 recognises that every approach to God by sinners needs covering.

debates.bearing: The two are not exclusive. Verse 4 names atonement, and the whole ritual expresses devotion. In Israel's worship the order was often sin offering, then burnt offering, then peace offering, Leviticus 9:7 and 9:22, so atonement and consecration belong together.

debates.question: Why is the bird offering handled so differently?

views.label: Practical necessity
views.case: A dove is too small to be skinned, quartered and arranged, so the priest does the work at the altar itself, wringing the head, draining the blood on the altar's side and tearing it by the wings, verses 15 to 17.

views.label: A deliberate provision for the poor
views.case: The law elsewhere presents birds as the option for those who cannot afford a lamb, Leviticus 5:7 and 12:8. The priest's larger share of the work means the poor worshiper is carried further by the priesthood, and the refrain of verse 17 is identical to that of verse 9.

debates.bearing: Both are true. The different handling arises from the nature of the bird, but the identical refrain is the theological point: God accepts the poor man's offering as fully as the rich man's.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 opens with the word adam, 'When any of you,' literally 'when a human being among you brings.' The law of the burnt offering is framed in the widest possible term, the same word as the first man in Genesis. The verb 'brings' is the causative form of qarav, 'to cause to come near,' so that verse 2 plays on one root three times: when a person 'brings near' an 'offering,' qorban, he 'brings near' from the herd or flock. Jesus cites the noun directly in Mark 7:11, 'Corban (that is, a gift devoted to God).'

The animal must be tamim, 'unblemished,' verses 3 and 10. The word means whole or complete, and it is the same adjective used of Noah, 'blameless in his generation,' Genesis 6:9, and in God's charge to Abram, 'Walk before Me and be blameless,' Genesis 17:1. What is required of the animal physically is required of the worshiper morally. Peter uses the matching language of Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19.

Acceptance is the key idea of verses 3 and 4. 'For its acceptance' translates a phrase built on ratson, favour or goodwill, and 'so it can be accepted' uses the related verb ratsah. The same pair recurs in Leviticus 22:19-20, where a defective animal 'will not be accepted on your behalf,' and in Isaiah 56:7, where the offerings of foreigners 'will be accepted on My altar.'

'Lay his hand' is samakh, to lean or press, a firm gesture rather than a light touch. Verse 4 has a single hand, while Leviticus 16:21 has Aaron lay 'both hands' and confess the people's sins.

'Make atonement' is kipper. Scholars debate its root sense. Some connect it with covering, others with wiping clean or purging, and it is closely linked to the noun kopher, ransom, used in Exodus 30:12 for 'a ransom for his life.' Leviticus 17:11 explains that 'it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul.' Each sense adds something: sin is covered, defilement is purged, and a life is given for a life.

'An offering made by fire' translates ishsheh. Most connect it with esh, fire, but some scholars link it to a word for gift, and a few modern versions render it 'food offering.' Finally, 'pleasing aroma,' reyach nichoach, contains a word from the root nuach, to rest or settle. It first appears after the flood, 'When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma,' Genesis 8:21, in a story whose hero's name, Noah, sounds like the same root.

typology.type: The whole animal burned on the altar
typology.fulfillment: Everything but the hide went up to God, Leviticus 1:9 and 7:8. Christ is the one whose whole life and death were given to the Father: 'I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:7, and He 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14. Paul uses the burnt offering's own phrase for the cross, 'a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. The escalation is that the animal had no will to give, while the Son laid down His life 'of My own accord,' John 10:18. The type falls short in repetition: the altar needed fresh offerings every morning, while He offered Himself 'once for all,' Hebrews 7:27.

typology.type: The ram offered in place of Isaac, Genesis 22:13
typology.fulfillment: The first burnt offering described in detail is the one God provided on Moriah. Isaac asked, 'where is the lamb for the burnt offering?' and Abraham answered, 'God Himself will provide the lamb,' Genesis 22:7-8. Leviticus 1 institutionalises that substitution. John the Baptist points to its fulfilment: 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29. The escalation is that God did not spare His own Son where He spared Abraham's. The type falls short because the ram could only stand in for one boy, while Christ gave His life 'as a ransom for many,' Matthew 20:28.

typology.type: The worshiper who offers and is accepted
typology.fulfillment: The goal of the burnt offering was that it be 'accepted on his behalf,' verse 4. In the New Testament believers themselves become the offering because they have first been accepted in Christ: 'offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God,' Romans 12:1. Paul even calls Christians 'the sweet aroma of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 2:15. The correspondence is real, but the order is reversed from any religion of earning. The Israelite brought the offering to be accepted; the Christian offers himself because the one sufficient offering has already been accepted for him.

typology.type: The fire that never went out, Leviticus 6:12-13
typology.fulfillment: The burnt offering was never finished; the fire burned day and night and was fed every morning. It pictured a continual need for atonement and a continual offering to God. Hebrews contrasts priests who 'stand' offering 'again and again the same sacrifices' with Christ who 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and 'sat down,' Hebrews 10:11-12. The escalation is from a sacrifice that must be renewed to one that is complete. The type falls short precisely where it was meant to: its endlessness pointed beyond itself to the offering that would end the need.

study.christ:
Hebrews gives the clearest line from this chapter to Christ. It takes Psalm 40, where David says, 'Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. Then I said, Here I am, I have come,' and hears it as the voice of the Son entering the world: 'a body You prepared for Me... I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:5-7. The point is not that the burnt offering was wrong, since Hebrews notes it was offered 'according to the law,' Hebrews 10:8. The point is that God always wanted what the animal could only picture, a whole person given over to His will. Jesus is that person. 'By that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,' Hebrews 10:10.

The details of the chapter help us see the shape of His offering. The animal had to be tamim, whole, and Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14. The worshiper's hand rested on its head so that it would be accepted 'on his behalf,' and Paul says 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The burnt offering went up as a pleasing aroma, and Christ 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2, the Old Testament phrase applied to the cross.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the thread of Moriah. The burnt offering Abraham was asked to make was his only son, Genesis 22:2, and God provided a ram instead. Paul seems to echo that scene when he says God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and the Lamb God provides at last is His own Son.

There is also the humble end of the chapter. The poor could bring a single turtledove or young pigeon, verse 14, and when Jesus was presented at the temple His parents offered 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' Luke 2:24. The One who would become the final offering was born into a household that could afford only the bird offering the law allowed the poor, Leviticus 12:8. He knows the poor worshiper's place from the inside.

We should keep the reading disciplined. The New Testament links Christ to the burnt offering as a whole, to its completeness, its substitution and its acceptance. It does not interpret the washing of the legs or the north side of the altar, and we need not either. What the chapter gives is the grammar of approach: a whole offering, a life for a life, and acceptance before God. Christ fulfils each part, and because His offering was accepted once for all, no one needs to bring another.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He speaks first. 'The LORD called to Moses and spoke to him,' verse 1. Israel did not work out how to approach God by trial and error. The way was revealed. God is not a mystery to be manipulated by ritual but a Person who tells His people how they may come.

He is holy, and His holiness is costly to approach. A life is given at every burnt offering. The fire never goes out, Leviticus 6:13. Blood is splashed against the altar on every side. The chapter does not let anyone imagine that sin is a small matter or that God can be approached without a death.

Yet He wants to receive. The whole chapter is aimed at acceptance, 'for its acceptance before the LORD,' verse 3, and it closes each case with 'a pleasing aroma.' That phrase does not mean God was hungry; Psalm 50:12-13 rules that out. It means He is pleased to accept the worshiper who comes His way. The God of Leviticus is not reluctant. He designs the way in because He wants His people near.

He is just and He is fair. The same holy standard, an unblemished male, applies to herd and flock, but the law bends toward those with little. A single bird is accepted with exactly the same words as a bull. God's holiness never becomes a wealth test. He sees the poor at His altar as clearly as the rich, a point Jesus Himself made about the widow's two coins, Mark 12:41-44.

He is also the God of the whole person. The burnt offering holds nothing back; everything goes up. God does not ask for a portion of His people's devotion while they keep the rest. That is why the later prophets could say that sacrifice without obedience is empty, Hosea 6:6, and why Paul speaks of the whole body offered, Romans 12:1.

The chapter holds together two things that are often pulled apart: judgment and grace. The animal dies because sin deserves death. The worshiper lives because God accepts a substitute. At the cross those two meet completely, and Leviticus 1 is one of the places where the church learns to see why.

For worship the chapter calls for awe and gladness together. We come to a God before whom a life must be given, and we come gladly, because He has provided and accepted the offering, and He receives us as a pleasing aroma in His Son.

crossReferences.note: Exodus ends with the glory filling the tabernacle and Moses unable to enter. Leviticus 1:1 begins with the LORD calling him and speaking from the tent. The burnt offering is the first answer to the problem of how sinners can approach so holy a presence.

Noah's burnt offerings after the flood are the first time Scripture uses the phrase 'pleasing aroma.' God responds by promising never again to curse the ground, even though the human heart is still evil. The burnt offering is tied from the beginning to mercy toward sinners.

Isaac asks where the lamb for the burnt offering is, and Abraham answers that God Himself will provide it. The ram caught in the thicket is offered 'in place of his son,' Genesis 22:13, the clearest early picture of the substitution Leviticus 1 builds into law.

The priests' instructions for the burnt offering. It stayed on the altar all night, the ashes were carried outside the camp, and the fire was fed every morning and never allowed to go out. It shows the burnt offering as the continual heartbeat of the sanctuary.

The law spells out what Leviticus 1:14-17 implies: a person who cannot afford a lamb may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering. God builds provision for the poor into His worship.

Mary and Joseph present Jesus at the temple and offer 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' the offering of those who cannot afford a lamb. The Son who would be the final sacrifice was born into a family that brought the poor person's offering.

David says God takes no pleasure in burnt offerings apart from a broken and contrite heart, and then that God will delight in 'whole burnt offerings' once the heart is right. The psalm shows that the burnt offering was meant to express repentance and faith, not replace them.

Samuel tells Saul that the LORD does not delight in burnt offerings as much as in obedience to His voice. Saul had kept animals to sacrifice after disobeying. The verse guards against using the offering of Leviticus 1 as a substitute for obeying God.

Hebrews reads Psalm 40 as the voice of Christ: God took no delight in burnt offerings, and so the Son came to do His will. Through the offering of His body once for all, believers are sanctified. The burnt offering is fulfilled in obedience embodied in a person.

Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God' through the eternal Spirit. The unblemished animal of Leviticus 1:3 finds its counterpart in the sinless Son, and His blood does what animal blood could not, cleansing the conscience so that we may serve the living God.

Paul describes Christ giving Himself up for us 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' borrowing the refrain of Leviticus 1:9, 13 and 17. The cross is the burnt offering God finally and fully accepts, and it becomes the pattern for the believer's walk in love.

On account of God's mercy, believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God. The whole offering of Leviticus 1 becomes the shape of Christian life, no longer an animal that dies but a person who lives wholly for God.

study.oneStory:
In Eden, the man and woman walked with God without any altar. After the fall the way back was guarded, and the first worship recorded outside the garden already involves offerings, Genesis 4:3-4. The burnt offering answers a question the story has been asking since Genesis 3: how can sinful people come near a holy God and live?

The answer grows through Genesis. Noah's burnt offering after the flood is received as a pleasing aroma, and God promises mercy on a world whose heart has not changed, Genesis 8:20-21. On Moriah God provides a ram in place of Abraham's son, Genesis 22:13. At Sinai God's glory comes to dwell in the tabernacle, and the problem becomes urgent, because now the holy God lives in the middle of the camp. Leviticus 1 is the first law He speaks from that tent. It turns the old practice of the burnt offering into the daily rhythm of a nation.

The chapter sets up much of what follows. The burnt offering is joined by the grain, peace, sin and guilt offerings, and together they shape Israel's worship until the temple falls. The prophets insist that the offerings must come from obedient hearts, and in the end they point beyond themselves, since the endless fire shows that the work is never done.

Christ brings the story to its turning point. He is the offering God always wanted, a whole life given to do His will, Hebrews 10:5-10, and He is the Lamb God Himself provides, John 1:29. His one offering does what the endless fire could not, and He sits down because the work is finished, Hebrews 10:12. Now His people offer themselves as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1.

The story ends in a city with no temple and no altar, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. No more burnt offerings are needed there, because the Lamb who was slain stands at the centre, Revelation 5:6, and the people He redeemed live in God's presence without fear.

quiz.q: What must the worshiper do before the burnt offering is slaughtered?

options.text: Lay his hand on the head of the offering, so it may be accepted to make atonement for him.
options.note: Verse 4 describes this act of identification between worshiper and sacrifice.

options.text: Recite a written prayer of confession.
options.note: No prayer is prescribed here; the text specifies the laying on of hands.

options.text: Wash himself in the courtyard first.
options.note: Washing belongs to the priestly preparation of the offering, not the worshiper's own act before slaughter.

options.text: Nothing; the priest handles the entire process alone.
options.note: The worshiper himself lays his hand on the animal and, in most cases, slaughters it.

quiz.q: What provision does God make for someone too poor to afford an animal from the herd or flock?

options.text: He may bring a turtledove or a young pigeon instead.
options.note: Verses 14 to 17 provide this offering of birds for the burnt offering.

options.text: He is exempt from bringing any offering.
options.note: The law does not exempt the poor; it scales the offering down to what they can afford.

options.text: He must borrow money to purchase a lamb.
options.note: The text provides an alternative offering rather than requiring debt.

options.text: No provision is made for the poor.
options.note: Verses 14 to 17 explicitly provide birds as an accessible offering.

quiz.q: What happens to the burnt offering on the altar?

options.text: The whole animal, except the hide, is burned completely as an offering made by fire.
options.note: This total consumption is what distinguishes the burnt offering, olah, from other sacrifices.

options.text: Only the fat portions are burned; the rest is eaten by the priests.
options.note: That pattern describes offerings like the peace offering, not the burnt offering, which is wholly consumed.

options.text: The animal is set free after the ritual.
options.note: The burnt offering is slaughtered and burned, not released.

options.text: Nothing is burned; the blood alone matters.
options.note: Both the blood and the whole animal have their prescribed place in the ritual.

quiz.q: What does the phrase 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD' communicate about the burnt offering?

options.text: That the offering, rightly brought, is accepted by God rather than rejected.
options.note: The phrase describes divine acceptance of the sacrifice, not a literal need for scent.

options.text: That God literally needs the smell of burning meat for nourishment.
options.note: Scripture elsewhere denies that God needs anything from His creatures, Psalm 50:12-13.

options.text: That the smoke had a pleasant fragrance to the worshipers nearby.
options.note: The phrase concerns God's acceptance, not the sensory experience of the human worshipers.

options.text: It has no theological significance.
options.note: The recurring phrase is a significant marker of the offering's acceptance before the LORD.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament interpret the burnt offering and sacrifices like it?

options.text: As unable to take away sin themselves, but pointing forward to Christ's once for all sacrifice.
options.note: Hebrews 10:1-10 makes exactly this argument about the old covenant sacrifices.

options.text: As a permanent pattern Christians must continue today.
options.note: Hebrews argues the opposite, that Christ's sacrifice ends the need for repeated offerings.

options.text: As having no connection to Christ whatsoever.
options.note: The New Testament repeatedly draws direct lines from these sacrifices to Christ's work.

options.text: As myths with no historical basis.
options.note: The New Testament treats these sacrifices as a real, historical system that finds its fulfillment in Christ.

questions: The worshiper laid his own hand on the offering before it died in his place. Where do you need to identify honestly with your need for a substitute rather than trusting your own good standing before God?
The burnt offering was wholly given, nothing held back. What parts of your life do you still hold back from full surrender to God?
God provided a way for the poor to bring an acceptable offering, birds instead of a bull. How does it change your view of God to know He has always made a way for the have not as much as the have?

This sacrifice had to be repeated again and again, yet Christ's sacrifice was offered once for all. Do you live as though your standing with God still depends on repeated effort, or do you rest in what is finished?
The whole system existed so people could draw near, qorban, to God. What keeps you from drawing near to Him today, and what would it look like to approach Him through Christ this week?

translationNotes.note: The LORD called to Moses translates a Hebrew verb that opens the book, tying Leviticus directly to the end of Exodus, where the glory of the LORD had just filled the newly completed tabernacle.
Make atonement for him translates kaphar, a verb whose root sense of covering or wiping away runs through the entire sacrificial system introduced in these opening chapters.
A pleasing aroma to the LORD is an anthropomorphic phrase describing divine acceptance of the offering; it does not imply that God requires food, compare Psalm 50:8-13.
